COMMODITIES RESEARCH 

11 February 2011 



# METALS MAGNIFIER 

# A road less travelled 



- In a fashion that would have an explorer green with envy, the metals are entering unchartered territory this year. Already, there have been a series of firsts, with new landmarks being set along the way. Copper has broken through $10,000/t, tin is well above $30,000/t, palladium is challenging ten-year highs, while aluminium and gold physical premiums are scaling record and multi-year highs, respectively. Also, importantly, the market has a newfound confidence in global economic growth. The perception that a wave of speculative money is the driving force behind the run-up in base metal prices is misplaced, in our view. Data show that some investment vehicles have in fact had outflows (such as physically backed ETFs), while CTFC and LME open interest data show that there is not a significant overhang of long positions. However, there is appetite from all segments of the industry to participate in the metals space this year.

- We are now at a crossroads, with the market in anticipation of a big pickup in buying and buyers in hope of lower prices; something will have to give. In particular, we will be watching for the quality of physical market indicators, not least LME stock trends and those relevant to the Chinese market, to improve. For now at least, the market appears to have come to terms with weakness in China’s post-holiday import buying, although we still view this as a short-term downside risk to prices. The road ahead is one less travelled, which means that price volatility is likely to remain elevated. But something is brewing, and we believe it is the beginning of a big increase in demand, which, together with a newfound confidence in the sustainability of economic growth, leads us to believe the route being mapped out is one of higher prices. For metals with positive fundamentals and whose market balances continue to tighten, we have revised our price forecasts higher to reflect this. Out in front, and by a big margin, are the trailbreakers copper and tin. With stocks-to-consumption ratios for these metals forecast to fall to record lows, set against a market with newfound confidence, we believe that prices will rise much further still, with copper prices expected to average more than $13,000/t by the end of the year. High prices have sparked discussion about the demand erosion that could be caused by substitution, which we look at in this month’s focus section.

#### **FOCUS** 

## **Almost irreplaceable** 

_Substitution is more than just a function of prices_ 

The run-up in copper prices to record highs has sparked discussion about the demand erosion that could be caused by substitution. Although there is evidence from the past that steep increases in prices can result in substitution, in our view concerns about the magnitude of potential demand losses for this year are excessive. Raw material decision making depends on a lot more than just price: factors such as price volatility, technological inferiority/superiority, competing product designs, regulatory changes and manufacturing location all contribute to the decision making process. That said, with copper’s main competitor, aluminium, trading at a quarter of copper’s level, the incentive to substitute is significant – although so far, consumer reports suggest that prices may have to rise much higher to spark any meaningful substitution. The primary market concern is the potential demand loss that could occur as a result of substitution. In this month’s focus piece, we take top-down and bottom-up approaches to analyse this topic, beginning with a sensitivity analysis of consumption, prices and economic growth, before getting more granular and delving into specific product areas in which substitution can and is taking place and identifying areas of high risk. Finally, to provide a well-rounded view, we have also included analysis of new end-use areas for copper, a part of the picture that is often ignored, which can result in unbalanced views. In all, our analysis shows there are a number of hurdles to substitution and that in reality there are only a few areas that pose real potential for demand losses, albeit over time. Given these hurdles, we believe that the effect of substitution on copper demand over the next few years will be to slow the pace of potential demand growth slightly. For instance, based on our forecast for the copper/aluminium price ratio to rise much further this year, our analysis suggests that demand growth could be dented by a mere 0.57%. 

_In contrast to the oil and agriculture markets, price sensitivity in the copper market is with the manufacturer not the consumer_

ts. For instance, in the case of oil, the consumer has direct exposure to the price at the pump and, in agriculture, the price of the foodstuff on the supermarket shelf. In the copper market, however, price sensitivity lies with the manufacturer, which bears the cost directly and has to compete with lower cost competitors, rather than the consumer since copper usually comprises only a small proportion of the overall cost of a product. In an environment of prices hitting record highs and expectations for prices to remain elevated for a prolonged period, manufacturers will step up efforts to reduce procurement and manufacturing costs. However, changing raw material usage is not a flippant decision for manufacturers because there are costs associated and hurdles to overcome. Long-held standards and practices and ongoing relationships between suppliers and specifiers are slow to change. The high cost of retooling and retraining employees can discourage manufacturers from switching to other materials. Furthermore, even if a competing commodity is trading at a lower price, the eventual price advantage may not be as great as initially perceived. For instance, in the wire and cable market, the larger size of an aluminium or copper-clad aluminium cable compared with a pure copper cable will need more insulation, shielding, armour and may be more complex to fabricate, all of which may offset the initial cost saving. That relationship has weakened considerably, as over the past five years, a 1% increase in global GDP led to less than a 1% increase in global copper consumption. ###### **Construction** 

- _The biggest end-use sector faces limited substitution risk_ 

_Regulatory and standard accepted practice hurdles will prevent major losses in the building wire sector_ 

- _Copper has lost significant market share in the plumbing sector_ 

The construction sector represents the source of greatest demand for copper, accounting for close to a third of total global consumption. Copper is used in a variety of areas such as building wire, plumbing and heating, as well as for architectural uses such as roofing. Despite construction being the area of largest use, the outlook for substitution risk here is limited, in our view, either because threats face significant qualitative hurdles or substitution effects are already close to completion because the case for the substitute has been persuasive for a long period of time. 

Perhaps the best example of the limited effect due to qualitative factors is in terms of building wire. In the case of household wiring, the issue with using aluminium, the obvious substitute from a cost basis, has been with the reliability of connectors. Despite attempts in the US in the 1960-70s to push for wholesale substitution towards aluminium building wire – indeed penetration resulted in copper reaching its lowest market share at 71.9% of the total insulated wire and cable market in 1974 – the shift was ultimately stymied by safety problems with its application. In the case of residential wiring, problems with aluminium connectors (typically referred to as EC aluminium) resulted in a series of fires (which the US Consumer Product Safety Commission highlighted). As a result, the industry standard since has been copper. This is not limited to the US: in other countries such as India, where aluminium building wire achieved deep penetration in the past, this trend has been fully reversed due to the same perception of low safety. Will

this move back to copper wire ever be reversed? Any substitution effects are unlikely in the short term, given that building regulation and codes would have to be amended, the sustained negative impressions of using alternatives and standard accepted procedures can be difficult to change. 

The second key area for consideration in construction is the plumbing sector. This is a case in which wholesale substitution towards plastic alternatives has been under way for a significant period. Plastic pipes and fittings are far less costly than copper, lighter and easier to install, as well as less liable to theft. While copper generally lasts longer and is more durable, plastics have now fully penetrated the piping market, and the majority of waste pipes carrying water away from sink drains and toilets are made of plastic. Copper still holds a key role in water distribution, although that could easily change in the future. In the mid2000s, substitution was particularly aggressive – in 2005 and 2006, 7% and 8%, respectively, of the copper plumbing market was lost to plastics. In our view, this was the period when the so-called “easy-wins” were completed. The latest ICA data indicate such

###### **Transportation** 

_Copper has been largely substituted out of the automotive radiator market_ 

The transportation market accounts for 13% of global copper consumption (2.8Mt), with copper used in almost every vehicle from family cars to heavy trucks, locomotives and aircraft using copper in wiring, cabling, motors, radiators and busbars. About 2% (9,000lbs, 4t) of the total weight of a Boeing 747-200 is copper, while a typical diesel-electric locomotive uses about 11,000 lbs (5t) and a typical US passenger car will use about 5570lbs (28Kg). In the transport sector, in particular for cars and aircraft, light-weighting is a key priority, so raw material decision making is not based purely on cost. Raw material usage patterns in the transportation sector can be more fluid than some other sectors due to the more regular and intensive research and development (R&D) undertaken b

y transportation companies, making this area potentially more open to substitution. One application in the transportation industry, where copper has been almost entirely substituted out of, is radiators. The trend first began in the mid-1960s when there was a large spike in the copper/aluminium price ratio (Figure 5). There was concerted development to engineer copper out of the radiators that was highly successful. _High risk areas for future substitution are battery cables and wire harnessing_ The areas of copper usage in the transportation market that we identify as being most at risk from substitution are battery cables and wire harnessing. Most automotive cables use copper conductors, though there have been some developments to use battery cables and wire harnessing with aluminium conductors. This is the area in which we expect the most rapid substitution. Aluminium has already made significant inroads into this sector, though we believe there is still potential for further, potentially sizeable, substitution. The quickest and most easily executed design change is to substitute round aluminium tube for round copper tube. The all-aluminium heat exchanger is also available and is the subject of continued development to improve design and technical competitiveness. In the developed European

As with many instances of substitution though, it is the developing markets that are using aluminium in this sector on a growing scale. We have heard anecdotal reports of substantial broad scale trials to shift to aluminium in Chinese air-conditioning manufacturing. This has been further evidenced by Brook Hunt reporting that Media, China’s largest air-conditioning manufacturer, has recently undertaken a trial to use aluminium alloy instead of copper tube for micro channel heat exchangers. 

###### **Industrial machinery** 

Copper is used in a variety of industrial machinery types such as in-plant equipment, industrial valves and fittings, non-electrical instruments, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers. This represented close to 13% (2.8Mt) of global demand in 2009. Apart from the risks of substitution in heat exchangers, which are sizeable, there is some evidence of substitution in terms of industrial vales and fittings, as copper brass rod has suffered from miniaturisation and lower copper alloys. Gears and bearings have experienced minimal substitution, but there is greater potential for substitution towards aluminium composites in turbine blades. That said, there is little evidence to suggest this is a key area for potential shifts. 

###### **Electric and electronic products** 

###### _Power utilities and lighting & wiring devices_ 

_The need for standardisation makes changes in raw material use very slow moving_ 

Electronics and electrical applications consume 6Mt of copper (the second largest end-use sector), accounting for 28% of demand. Within that sector, competing materials have made inroads in the power cable market, but only to a limited degree given the necessary technical specifications, such as conductivity. However, preferences vary across the world, with Indian and Brazilian power utilities preferring aluminium conductors to copper in insulated power cables. Given the need for national standardisation, it is more challenging to change raw material usage in the power cable market. A key problem in this area is that it is more difficult to link an aluminium cable with a copper network and connections. For this reason, industrial users of power cables are more likely than utilities to prefer copper conductors as contractors may not have the specialist skills needed for installing cables with aluminium conductors. There is a need for standardisation that is a limiting factor in changes in raw material usage. Although there is plenty of potential for substitution in power utilities, this sector is generally slow in making technical changes. Favoured cable designs once established will be retained for a long time. 

The market is generally divided into three categories: low-voltage (LV), medium-voltage (MV) and high-voltage (HV). 

- Low voltage – used for conne

ction between a residential or small commercial customer and the utility. In the LV market, copper clad aluminium cables (CCA) have made inroads, especially in the emerging markets such as China and India, with Chinese

- Medium voltage (distribution) – used for distribution in urban and rural areas. Copper wires are commonly used in MV distribution to premises, though in newer markets aluminium is making inroads. 

- High voltage (subtransmission and transmission) – used for transmission of bulk quantities of electric power and connection to very large consumers. The bare wire conductors on the line are generally made of aluminium (either plain or reinforced with steel or sometimes composite materials). Aluminium conductors reinforced with steel (known as ACSR) are primarily used for MV and HV lines and may also be used for overhead services to individual customers. Aluminium conductors are used because it has better resistivity/weight than copper, as well as being cheaper, requiring less supports and being more wind resistant. 

Copper clad aluminium (CCA) wire and cable has grown in popularity over the past few years, in particular in the emerging markets, which have huge infrastructure build needs. In developed markets, CCA wiring is more commonly used in the form of enamelled magnet wire with inroads increasingly being made in applications such as headphones and aircraft instruments (where weight saving is a priority). In coaxial cables, the high frequency signal is transmitted in the surface layers, and therefore the aluminium (or in some cases steel) wire core does not detract from the absolute performance. 

_Emerging markets have little or no standard accepted practises so offer the best potential to implement different products_ 

But, as with many of the changes in raw material usage, emerging markets are leading the way in large part because there are generally fewer or no standard accepted practices, making it easier to implement new or different technologies. CCA consists of copper cladding surrounding an aluminium core, or in the case of CAA wiring, the aluminium wires are copper coated. The most common grade of CCA contains 10% copper by volume and has 65% of the conductivity of an equivalent all-copper cable. Given its inferior conductivity, CCA is only used in certain applications. A key consideration is that CCA cable has a much wider diameter than a pure copper cable. This characteristic, together with its comparatively light weight, means they are more commonly used in overhead applications than underground. However, one of the main drawbacks of using aluminium wires and cables is that they need specially designed accessories to give reliable electrical connections. Cable-specialis

t knowledge is required, making wide-scale implementation difficult. Another factor that has restricted more penetration of CAA wiring and cable in developed markets is a limited number of suppliers. However, the massive growth in production of this product in China means it has become more widely available in recent years. Cost is clearly the key consideration when choosing a CCA cable, yet the savings are not as straightforward as the difference between the copper and aluminium prices. A CCA cable is more complicated to fabricate and so has higher fabrication costs, as well as higher auxiliary input costs due to its larger size than a pure copper cable. That said, these additional costs are more than offset in a market in which copper is trading at four times the cost of aluminium. 

Although the scope for potential substitution in the power cable and wiring devices markets is large, we view this as only a medium-risk area given the challenges faced in changing component parts in this area. Aluminium’s inferior conductivity is a significant drawback, while the need for standardisation and considerations of size add further hurdles to using materials other than copper. Substitution in this area tends to be slower moving than other sectors, so we expect net losses in consumption to be marginal over the next two years.

###### _Telecommunication cable_ 

_Copper’s usage in telecoms has already declined dramatically_ 

Along with plumbing in the building and construction sector, copper usage in telecommunications has declined significantly due to substitution over the past decade. While cost inevitably played a part, technical performance was the main reason. Fibre optic cables have largely displaced copper telecom cables in a number of applications, such as trunk telecom networks, because they give a superior performance with higher productivity. So far it has largely involved long distance trunk lines, while the local connection has until recently remained copper. 

With well-established routes for substitution, together with the superior technical performance of competing materials such as fibre optics, we believe further substitution in this sector could be substantial. However, given that copper has already lost a lot of market share, the net effect on tonnage consumed is likely to be small. 

###### _Electronics_ 

_The technical demands of semiconductors means manufacturers are increasingly using copper_ 

Unlike the other sectors we have discussed, electronic is the only sector in which there has been a broad shift from aluminium towards copper. Major electronic manufacturers have increasingly been engineering copper into their products in recent years as aluminium had previously been used due to shifting technical demands. The need for smaller, faster and more energy efficient components is increasingly rendering aluminium as an inferior raw material. Aluminium’s low mechan

ical strength means it can crack when it becomes stressed, which is in direct conflict with the increasing volumes of stress semiconductors are subjected to. This problem has been exacerbated by the demand for semiconductors to become smaller in size. For these reasons, copper is increasingly favoured as a superior raw material for semiconductors because it has higher mechanical strength, is more ductile and has superior electrical conductivity. The result is faster operating speeds and greater circuit integration. First, the move towards greener, more energy-efficient economies is a policy shift that stands to benefit copper, given its quality as an excellent conductor and heat transferor. Certainly, while copper may lose out to aluminium in terms of weight, electric and hybrid vehicles still use two to three times more copper than in standard equivalent-sized vehicles. For example, the new electric vehicles from Ford Motor Company, including their hybrid electric, battery electric (that are all electric) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (run on a battery plus gas engine), use more copper for all of their high and low voltage wiring and in the motor winding than in your average ‘non electric’ vehicle. Indeed, more than half of the 68-82Kg of copper used in electric cars is in the wiring harness and electrical components. The inverter system (to deliver power to the motors) alone uses 8-18Kg. The additional copper is needed because the motor in electric vehicles is much larger and the wiring needs to carry a higher current and voltage. Within the green theme, new sources of renewable power also are well leveraged to copper’s energy efficiency. For example, in wind turbines, copper used in the grounding of the towe

rs in the event of lightning transports electricity to substations and connects the system into the utility grid. Given that the turbines are often located far from substations, the length of copper wiring and cabling needed is massive. This is particularly the case for offshore wind turbines, which require huge lengths of undersea cabling. Copper also plays a critical role in the turbine motors and their control wires. Onshore wind farms can require 6t of copper per MW of generating capacity, or a total of 16t per turbine. Split by usage, 5t is contained in the turbine and its transformer, while 11t is contained in the cabling. Offshore wind farms require even greater volumes of copper with 31t of copper per turbine, which is 10t per MW. In addition, moves towards greener power grids such as the ‘smart grid’ roll out in the US should provide a key driver for copper given its conductivity quality.

Xstrata’s Mt Isa zinc mining and smelting facilities, which produce 345Ktpy zinc in concentrate, were reduced to a skeleton staff.
